items.philosophy-equation-df083bc202: This defines a deterministic toy world: the next physical state is obtained by applying a transition rule F to the current state and action, while the observation is produced by a sensor rule O applied to the current state. The distinction matters because the observation may hide parts of the state, so predicting from a picture alone can be impossible even when the underlying state evolves simply.
items.geometry-equation-e39ce4f70f: This simple encoder takes a four-entry observation and returns a two-entry latent vector. Its first coordinate adds the first-row pixel values, and its second coordinate adds the second-row pixel values, so it keeps row totals while discarding left–right position within each row.
items.geometry-equation-7d3eb3e066: The matrix W is the row-sum encoder written as a linear map. Multiplying W by the observation column makes each output coordinate a weighted sum of input pixels: the first row adds the first two entries, and the second row adds the last two entries. This shows how an encoder can be represented as coordinated measurements of the input.
items.geometry-equation-306632ccb4: Multiplying the column x by the row y transpose creates a two-by-two outer product, whose entries are all pairwise products of coordinates from x and y. With x equal to one, two and y equal to three, four, the rows become three, four and six, eight. This differs from the dot product, which would collapse the two vectors to a single number.
items.geometry-equation-784861ff4b: This expands the squared distance from x to the point c times u on a line. Using the dot product, the middle terms combine to negative two c times u transpose x, and because u is a unit vector, the final factor u transpose u becomes one. This prepares the distance for finding the closest point on the line.
items.geometry-equation-6d965a8cc4: This rewrites the same squared distance by completing the square in the scalar c. The only part that changes with c is the square of c minus u transpose x, so the distance is smallest when c equals u transpose x. That value is the signed scalar projection of x along the unit direction u.
items.probability-equation-170eebd893: This computes the variance of the sample mean for B independent samples with common variance sigma squared. Expanding the variance of the average gives a double sum of covariances; independence makes all off-diagonal covariances zero, leaving B diagonal terms. Dividing by B squared gives sigma squared over B, the usual variance reduction from averaging independent data.
items.probability-equation-4b306a073e: This is the density of a standard Gaussian random variable, centered at zero with unit scale. The exponential term gives the bell shape, assigning smaller density to values farther from zero, while the factor one over the square root of two pi normalizes the total area to one.
items.probability-equation-ba31d1e9c0: Here, I is the one-dimensional area under the unnormalized Gaussian curve, and squaring it turns the product of two identical one-dimensional integrals into an integral over the whole plane. This matters because the two-dimensional form depends only on distance from the origin, which makes the normalization constant easier to compute using circular geometry.
items.probability-equation-541e6ee4f7: The two-dimensional integral is rewritten in polar coordinates: angle contributes a full factor of two pi, and radius contributes the factor r in the area element. Substituting v equals r squared over two turns r dr into dv, leaving the integral of e to the minus v from zero to infinity, which equals one; therefore I squared is two pi.
items.probability-equation-97606876ef: This derivation computes the variance of the standard Gaussian, since the mean is zero and variance is the integral of x squared times the density p. The identity p prime equals minus x times p changes the integral into one suited for integration by parts; the boundary term vanishes because the Gaussian tail decays very fast, and the remaining integral of p is one.
items.clouds-equation-549f7a4f57: This identity splits the total squared distance from the batch points to any candidate center c into two parts: the spread around the batch mean, plus B times the squared distance from c to that mean. The cross term disappears because centered deviations sum to zero, so only the last term depends on c, proving the mean is the distance-minimizing center.
items.clouds-equation-6e87d43756: This defines the batch covariance matrix C as the average outer product of each centered example with itself. Writing it as one over B times X c transpose X c is the same calculation in matrix form, and it packages the cloud’s coordinate variances and pairwise co-variations into one object.
items.clouds-equation-cb29a42b9b: Multiplying the covariance matrix on both sides by a direction u gives the average squared projection of the centered data onto that direction. In plain terms, it is the variance of the cloud when measured along u, which is why this quantity can never be negative.
items.clouds-equation-d663419836: The centered batch matrix has at most d independent columns and, because its B rows sum to zero, at most B minus one independent rows. Therefore its rank cannot exceed the smaller of d and B minus one, a structural limit caused by centering the particular batch.
items.clouds-equation-6bc791cc24: This example gives a simple two-by-two covariance matrix and two unit directions: the rising diagonal u and the falling diagonal v. Multiplying by the matrix shows these directions are eigenvectors, so the cloud’s spread is measured cleanly along them, with no rotation into another direction.
items.clouds-equation-6d5d6aae87: The matrix Q stores the two principal directions as its columns, and Lambda stores their variances, 3 and 1, on the diagonal. The factorization C equals Q Lambda Q transpose says that the covariance can be built by moving into principal-direction coordinates, scaling by the variances along those directions, and moving back to the original coordinates.
items.clouds-equation-b32761916a: This is the density of a d-dimensional standard Gaussian, whose coordinates are independent standard normal variables. Multiplying the one-dimensional densities gives the constant factor involving 2 pi, and the exponent uses the squared length of x, so the probability density depends only on distance from the origin, not on direction.
items.clouds-equation-8d5f5cafef: This computes the covariance after whitening the centered vector: first rotate into the eigenvector coordinates with Q transpose, then divide each principal coordinate by the square root of its variance. Since C equals Q Lambda Q transpose, the middle product becomes Lambda, and the two inverse square-root factors turn it into the identity covariance.
items.calculus-equation-0aaa885c25: This ratio is the average output change per unit input change for f of x equals x squared over a step h. Expanding the square leaves 2 x plus h, so as the step shrinks, the extra h disappears and the local conversion factor becomes the derivative, 2 x.
items.calculus-equation-0c8d5a4806: This rewrites the change in a product as two contributions: the change in v multiplied by the new value of u, plus the change in u multiplied by the old value of v. Dividing by h and then shrinking h separates the two local effects, which leads to the product rule for derivatives.
items.calculus-equation-2d5c5f75a2: This measures how the loss changes when only w is increased by h while b is held fixed. Because the prediction uses 2w, the error changes from e to e plus 2h; expanding the squared loss gives a linear term, 2 e h, and a smaller quadratic term, 2 h squared, whose limit yields the partial derivative with respect to w.
items.calculus-equation-6a4514b637: The gradient collects the two partial derivatives of the loss into one column vector. Its first entry, 2e, is the sensitivity to w, and its second entry, e, is the sensitivity to b, so it records how small separate parameter changes affect the loss at the current point.
items.calculus-equation-23285da809: This exact expansion separates the loss change from changing both parameters into a first-order part and a curvature correction. The dot product of the gradient with delta gives the local linear prediction, while the final squared term accounts for the remaining quadratic effect of the combined change in w and b.
items.calculus-equation-6988e14098: For a small parameter displacement delta from theta, the loss is approximated by its current value plus the gradient dot delta, with a remainder that becomes negligible compared with the step length as the step shrinks. This formalizes the idea that the dot product gives the first-order change, while higher-order curvature effects are smaller locally.
items.calculus-equation-eed2097208: When x first changes an intermediate value f of x and that intermediate value then changes y through g, the total sensitivity is the product of the two local sensitivities. The derivative of y with respect to x is therefore the derivative of the outside function evaluated at f of x, times the derivative of the inside function.
items.calculus-equation-f969e0c89d: The Jacobian records every local input-output sensitivity: row i and column j contains the partial derivative of output component f i with respect to input component x j. Multiplying this table by a small input change gives the first-order predicted change in all outputs at once.
items.calculus-equation-a681965a96: For the function with outputs x one times x two and x one plus x two, the Jacobian has one row per output. The product output changes with x one at rate x two and with x two at rate x one, while the sum output changes at rate one with respect to each input.
items.calculus-equation-756ebee36d: For a composed map, the Jacobian of the whole transformation is the Jacobian of the outer map, evaluated at the intermediate value f of x, multiplied by the Jacobian of the inner map. This is the many-input, many-output chain rule: local effects pass through the intermediate layer by matrix multiplication.
items.calculus-equation-7bff5d19e4: A scalar loss changes by the output-gradient dotted with the output change; substituting the linearized output change J f times delta x gives the first expression. Regrouping the dot product moves J f onto the gradient as a transpose, showing why backward sensitivities are computed with J f transpose times the output sensitivity.
items.calculus-equation-564088347d: This Hessian is the table of second derivatives for the loss one half times the square of two w plus b minus five. Its entries say how the gradient changes with w and b, and its quadratic form produces the curvature correction one half times two delta w plus delta b squared.
items.calculus-equation-2c2670d514: The vector move from x in direction v is rewritten as a one-dimensional path r of t. Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus twice expresses the endpoint value as the starting value, plus the initial slope, plus a weighted integral of the second derivative along the path; that integral is the exact accumulated curvature contribution.
items.calculus-equation-04f9bf1a38: This is the second-order Taylor approximation for a scalar loss after a small vector displacement v. The loss changes by its current value, plus a linear gradient term, plus a curvature term using the Hessian matrix, with a remaining error that becomes negligible compared with the square of the step size when v shrinks.
items.calculus-equation-fe52484ba4: These two Taylor expansions describe the function value a small distance h to the right and to the left of x. The first-derivative term changes sign between the plus and minus cases, while the second-derivative term stays the same; that symmetry is what later lets the central difference cancel even-order or odd-order pieces as needed.
items.learning-equation-ca18706ed3: These derivatives say how the squared prediction error changes when the shared parameters w and b are nudged. The bias derivative is just the prediction error, while the weight derivative is that same error multiplied by the input x, because w affects the prediction through the product w times x.
items.learning-equation-c5a509b5d5: GELU defines an activation by multiplying the input x by Phi of x, the standard-Gaussian cumulative probability up to x. This makes a smooth gate: positive inputs are mostly kept, negative inputs are mostly reduced, and the probability function is only being used to shape the nonlinearity, not to claim the network features are Gaussian probabilities.
items.learning-equation-c90d720e66: This lays out the forward computation for a two-layer scalar-output network. The first layer forms pre-activation values from the input, the activation produces hidden features, the second layer combines those features into a prediction, and the loss measures squared prediction error against the target; backpropagation will apply the chain rule through this sequence in reverse.
items.learning-equation-df940e3573: Delta is the hidden-layer sensitivity: the output error is passed back through the second-layer weights and then multiplied coordinate by coordinate by the activation derivative. The gradient for the first-layer weight matrix is the outer product of this sensitivity with the input, and the bias gradient is just the same sensitivity because each bias adds directly to one pre-activation.
items.learning-equation-efabdf16e0: Adam keeps two running averages at step k: m tracks recent gradients, and v tracks recent coordinatewise squared gradients. The beta factors control how much past information is retained, so persistent gradient directions accumulate while the squared-gradient average records the typical scale of updates in each coordinate.
items.learning-equation-50b66c9c3e: These lines apply Adam’s bias correction and then update the parameters. Since the running averages start at zero, m and v are divided by one minus the appropriate beta power; the parameter step then moves opposite the corrected gradient average, scaled coordinatewise by the square root of the corrected squared-gradient average plus epsilon.
items.learning-equation-cfdde1cea9: This objective measures the squared training errors of the scalar predictor w times x, then adds lambda times w squared as a penalty for large weight magnitude. The condition lambda at least zero makes the penalty nonnegative, so it expresses a preference for smaller weights rather than adding new information from the observations.
items.learning-equation-3f49e697ee: The fitted scalar weight w star is the data alignment, the sum of each input times its target, divided by the input energy plus the regularization strength lambda. The extra lambda in the denominator shrinks the weight toward zero; this is the algebraic form of trading some training fit for the prior preference for smaller magnitude.
items.learning-equation-700dee1b5a: These normal equations are the vector version of the scalar optimum: the matrix X transpose X summarizes how input features co-vary, lambda times the identity adds the weight penalty, and X transpose y summarizes alignment with targets. Solving this linear system gives the regularized least-squares weights, with positive lambda also making the left-hand matrix safely invertible.
items.learning-equation-2b2506c434: This central difference estimates the derivative of the loss with respect to coordinate j by nudging theta a small amount forward and backward along the j-th basis direction. Dividing the change in loss by twice the perturbation cancels the leading symmetric error terms, making it a useful numerical check of an analytic gradient when epsilon is chosen carefully.
items.jepa-equation-ad26c67ef5: This derivative follows both routes by which the shared encoder parameters theta affect the squared residual: through the context observation passed into the predictor, and through the target observation being predicted. The two contributions have opposite signs because the residual is prediction minus target embedding, which is why a learnable target branch can move unless a stop-gradient deliberately removes that path.
items.jepa-equation-d45112a18b: This contrastive loss treats the related view as the correct class among one positive score and K negative scores. The exponentials and temperature tau turn scores into a softmax probability, and the negative logarithm penalizes the model when the positive pair does not receive a large share of that probability.
items.jepa-equation-e248f23b51: This gradient says that each score is pushed according to its current softmax probability p j, with an extra subtraction for the positive score. Under gradient descent, the positive score is increased because its derivative includes minus one, while negative scores are decreased in proportion to how much probability they currently receive.
items.jepa-equation-ce6b24551d: This update makes the target parameters bar theta an exponential moving average of the online parameters theta across optimization steps. The coefficient m controls inertia: values near one keep the target branch changing slowly, while smaller values make it follow the online branch more quickly.
items.jepa-equation-af71428b74: The variance loss averages, over the d embedding coordinates, a hinge penalty for any coordinate whose batch standard deviation sigma j falls below the chosen floor gamma. Coordinates with enough spread contribute zero, while nearly constant coordinates are penalized, so this term helps prevent the learned representation Z from collapsing to the same value for every example.
items.jepa-equation-e2c1f4eea2: The covariance loss averages the squared off-diagonal entries of the centered batch covariance matrix C for one branch of embeddings Z. It penalizes linear redundancy between different coordinates, not the variance of a coordinate with itself; squaring makes both positive and negative cross-covariances count as unwanted dependence rather than allowing cancellation.
items.jepa-equation-0526e3a414: When the variance hinge is active, this is the derivative of the penalty with respect to one batch value x i: it is proportional to that value’s deviation from the batch mean, divided by the current standard-deviation-like term. Under gradient descent, above-mean values are pushed higher and below-mean values lower, but if all values are exactly equal then every numerator is zero, creating the caveat about a collapsed point with no escape gradient.
items.jepa-equation-6cbee7f9cd: The prediction loss averages squared coordinate errors between the predicted next embedding, hat z, and the encoded next observation, z, across batch items, time transitions, and embedding dimensions. This matters because temporal world models should not force consecutive observations to have identical embeddings; instead, the predictor uses context and the correctly aligned action for the transition to match the next representation.
items.testing-equation-fd7261af71: Phi of x is the cumulative distribution function of a standard Gaussian: it adds up the bell-curve density from negative infinity up to x. In plain terms, it gives the probability that a standard normal random variable is at or below x, which is the reference curve used for comparison with empirical observations.
items.testing-equation-ab604559ea: D n is the largest vertical distance, over all real x, between the empirical cumulative distribution F n and the standard-Gaussian cumulative distribution Phi. This Kolmogorov–Smirnov discrepancy compares accumulated probability rather than histogram bins, so it measures the worst mismatch between the observed sample distribution and the fully specified Gaussian reference.
items.testing-equation-e52f201030: After sorting the sample values, the largest Kolmogorov–Smirnov gap can be computed by checking each jump of the empirical cumulative curve. For the i-th sorted value, one candidate gap is just after the jump, i over n minus Phi at that value, and the other is just before the jump, Phi at that value minus i minus 1 over n; the maximum over all candidates gives D n.
items.testing-equation-994db3d3c7: This Monte Carlo p-value estimates the upper-tail rank of the observed discrepancy among R simulated null discrepancies plus the observed one. It counts how many simulated discrepancies are at least as large as the observed value, adds one to avoid an artificial zero and respect exchangeability, then divides by R plus one; using greater-than-or-equal is conservative when ties occur.
items.sigreg-equation-61791f1ea4: For any density p with mean zero and identity covariance, the KL divergence from the standard Gaussian p zero equals negative entropy of p plus the two Gaussian constants shown here. The expected squared length contributes d, producing the final d over two term; this connects KL nonnegativity to the fact that the standard Gaussian has the largest entropy among densities with those moments.
items.sigreg-equation-fc8cf7cc9c: The squared magnitude of the complex number a plus i b is found by multiplying it by its complex conjugate, a minus i b. The mixed terms cancel and i squared equals negative one, leaving a squared plus b squared, the ordinary squared distance of the point from the origin.
items.sigreg-equation-3496f0eef5: Euler’s identity says that the complex exponential with imaginary input i times t lands on the unit circle at angle t. Its real coordinate is cosine of t and its imaginary coordinate is sine of t, which lets later measurements turn real samples into unit arrows in the complex plane.
items.sigreg-equation-54793ff751: The complex exponential is expanded using its power series, then the even powers and odd powers are separated. Even powers of i produce alternating real terms, matching the cosine series, while odd powers leave one factor of i times an alternating sine series; this is the algebra behind Euler’s identity.
items.sigreg-equation-592eec2c6b: This differentiates the Gaussian characteristic function with respect to the frequency. The derivative brings down a factor i times x inside the integral, and the standard Gaussian identity p prime equals negative x times p rewrites the x p term as negative p prime, preparing the expression for integration by parts.
items.sigreg-equation-336e6ed90f: After integration by parts, the boundary term disappears because the Gaussian density goes to zero while the complex exponential stays bounded. Differentiating the exponential with respect to x contributes i times the frequency, so the derivative of the characteristic function equals negative frequency times the characteristic function itself.
items.sigreg-equation-e01d4fb9cc: For Y equal to a shift mu plus a scale sigma times a standard Gaussian X, the characteristic function splits into a rotation factor and a Gaussian decay factor. The shift mu creates the complex phase e to the i mu frequency, while the scale sigma changes the decay rate through sigma squared times frequency squared.
items.sigreg-equation-85a6ad5125: The empirical characteristic function estimates the population fingerprint at a chosen frequency by averaging the unit complex arrows from a batch of B scalar projections. Its real part C is the average cosine and its imaginary part S is the average sine, giving a batch statistic without estimating a density.
items.sigreg-equation-3c22832cef: At a fixed frequency, the empirical characteristic function has average cosine C as its real part and average sine S as its imaginary part. Because the Gaussian target is real, the squared distance between the empirical arrow and the target is the real error, C minus the target, squared, plus the sine part squared.
items.sigreg-equation-ad8d0bb0e0: The batch discrepancy disc sub B adds up the squared fingerprint error across all frequencies. The positive window w decides how much each frequency counts; in this chapter it downweights high frequencies, making the integral finite while still comparing the averaged sample arrows to the target fingerprint.
items.sigreg-equation-eb1a202d86: This expands the expected squared error of the empirical mean at one frequency. After subtracting the true mean mu from each sample arrow Y sub b, the squared magnitude of the average becomes a double sum over all pairs of batch indices, with one term conjugated because the quantities are complex.
items.sigreg-equation-d78765b4c7: For independent samples, all off-diagonal pair terms vanish because each centered arrow has mean zero. The B diagonal terms each contribute one minus the squared magnitude of the true characteristic function, so dividing by B squared leaves the expected empirical characteristic-function error equal to that variance term divided by the batch size.
items.sigreg-equation-6ffc9a2cf4: When the population is already standard Gaussian, integrating the one-frequency sampling error against the Gaussian window gives the expected unscaled discrepancy. It shrinks like one over B, while the scaled statistic stat sub B, defined as B times disc sub B, has the constant expected value shown here.
items.sigreg-equation-0209480368: The scalar projection proj sub b is the dot product of the learned embedding lat sub b with a chosen direction uvec, written as a coordinate-by-coordinate weighted sum. Requiring uvec to have unit length means different directions are compared on the same measurement scale, rather than stretching or shrinking the projection.
items.sigreg-equation-8b2206e5b2: For a vector Z with independent standard Gaussian coordinates, the characteristic function of any unit projection factors into a product over coordinates. Each coordinate contributes a scalar Gaussian factor, the exponents add, and the unit-length condition makes the sum of squared direction weights equal one, leaving the standard Gaussian fingerprint.
items.sigreg-equation-48a4a6b74c: This identity writes a d-dimensional Gaussian bump of width epsilon, centered at y and evaluated at x, as an inverse Fourier integral over frequency vectors v. It is the smoothing bridge used in the uniqueness argument: after adding Gaussian noise, densities can be expressed in terms of characteristic functions.
items.sigreg-equation-fafd8c9f19: This formula gives the density of the smoothed random vector X plus epsilon times G, where G is a standard Gaussian noise vector. It is the Fourier inversion integral for the characteristic function of X multiplied by the Gaussian damping factor; the damping makes the integral well behaved and lets equal characteristic functions imply equal smoothed densities.
items.sigreg-equation-73989e0200: This inequality bounds the expected difference D epsilon by splitting outcomes into two cases. When D epsilon is at most delta, the contribution is no more than delta; on the remaining event, boundedness of f gives the crude bound two M, weighted by the probability of that event. This turns pointwise convergence into convergence of expectations.
items.sigreg-equation-b8470a9337: These alpha k values are the numerical integration weights after using symmetry and the trapezoid rule on the nonnegative frequency interval. The two endpoints are counted once, giving weight Delta, while each interior sample belongs to two neighboring trapezoids and gets weight two Delta.
items.sigreg-equation-4b0461e2ba: This bounds the Gaussian tail discarded when frequencies beyond positive cutoff A are ignored. On that tail, omega is at least A, so the exponential can be bounded using omega divided by A. Integrating the resulting derivative of the exponential of negative omega squared over two leaves that same exponential evaluated at A, divided by A.
items.sigreg-equation-c06d8b38a4: This closed form computes the unscaled, untruncated one-dimensional discrepancy from the projected batch values using Gaussian integrals instead of a frequency grid. The first sum compares every pair of projected samples, the second sum is the cross term between the empirical characteristic function and the Gaussian target, and the final constant is the target-squared term.
items.sigreg-equation-76ea4f9030: This derivative tells how the one-direction statistic changes when one projected sample proj b moves. Each frequency contributes a chain-rule term from the cosine average and the sine average; the outer batch factor cancels the one over B from differentiating the batch means, while the Gaussian target contributes no derivative.
items.sigreg-equation-01e89bf142: This applies the chain rule from projected coordinates back to the learned latent coordinate lat b,j. For each direction m, the derivative with respect to the projection H b,m is multiplied by the projection matrix entry U j,m, and the results are averaged over the M sampled directions.
items.sigreg-equation-f54fb8fa1f: This expansion studies a tiny spread away from the collapsed cloud by writing each projection as s times a fixed centered pattern. The leading change is quadratic in s and negative whenever the frequency grid has a nonzero contribution, so a small nonzero spread can lower the regularizer even though the first derivative at exact collapse is zero.
items.implementation-equation-7bf521d140: The predicted next embedding is defined as the current learned embedding plus a residual correction produced by the network r psi. That correction may use the two recent embeddings and the two recent actions, so if the network outputs zero the predictor reduces to persistence: it predicts no latent change.
items.implementation-equation-895aaaeab2: The prediction loss is the mean squared error between each predicted future embedding coordinate and the corresponding encoded next embedding coordinate. The sums run over the batch examples and embedding coordinates, and division by B times d makes the scale an average per coordinate rather than a total.
items.implementation-equation-00e7463d3e: The participation ratio turns the covariance eigenvalues into an effective number of active directions. Squaring the total variance and dividing by the sum of squared directional variances gives a value near one when variance is concentrated in one direction, and equals r when r positive eigenvalues are equal.
items.laboratory-equation-f950558f6d: The total loss has two parts: an averaged squared prediction error over B examples and d embedding coordinates, plus a regularization term averaged over the three sequence positions. The coefficient lambda is set to 0.01 for these exact reductions, so changing the averaging convention would change the balance between prediction accuracy and the regularizer.
items.planning-equation-f727e995bf: A planning rollout starts by setting the first predicted latent state to the current encoded observation. The fixed learned dynamics model g psi is then applied H times, each time using the current predicted state and the proposed action, giving H transitions, H actions, and a final predicted state at time t plus H.
items.planning-equation-a242018fee: This planning objective combines terminal goal matching with an action-effort penalty. The first term measures squared distance between the final predicted embedding and the goal embedding, while the second adds the squared sizes of all proposed actions, weighted by the nonnegative coefficient rho.
items.planning-equation-05ebbfebd5: This backward recursion propagates sensitivity of the terminal cost through the learned dynamics. At step k, the next sensitivity vector is multiplied by the transpose of the dynamics Jacobian with respect to the encoded state, which is the chain rule used in backpropagation through time.
items.planning-equation-6c54ba13e2: For one action coordinate, this likelihood treats the elite values as independent samples from a Gaussian with mean mu and positive standard deviation sigma. CEM refits the sampling distribution by choosing parameters that make these elite values dense under the Gaussian, which leads after taking logs to the elites’ sample mean and variance.
items.planning-equation-44a63a7c26: This is the negative log likelihood for the elite action samples under a one-dimensional Gaussian with mean mu and standard deviation sigma. Taking logs turns the product of independent Gaussian densities into a sum: a constant normalizing term, a log sigma term, and a squared-error term measuring how far the selected actions are from the proposed mean. Minimizing this expression gives the Gaussian refit used by CEM.
items.planning-equation-de9b303bec: The fitted variance v star is the average squared distance of the elite actions from their fitted mean mu star. The denominator is the number of elites, not one less, because this is the maximum-likelihood refit for the selected samples, rather than an unbiased estimate of a larger population variance. In CEM, this variance controls how widely the next round samples around the promising plans.
items.planning-equation-e2e18badaa: This bounds the next rollout error by splitting it into two parts: sensitivity to starting from the imagined latent state instead of the encoded true latent state, plus the learned model’s one-step transition error. The Lipschitz assumption turns the first part into L times the current error, and the assumed one-step error bound contributes epsilon. This explains how small teacher-forced errors can accumulate during imagined rollouts.
items.evaluation-equation-9590101c03: Pearson correlation compares how the probe’s predictions and the targets vary together after subtracting their sample means. The numerator is their centered co-variation, and the two denominator factors rescale by the amount of variation in predictions and targets. This makes correlation insensitive to overall scale and offset, so it measures aligned variation rather than calibrated numerical accuracy.
items.evaluation-equation-9e90f26dd3: These formulas define the high-dimensional neighbor probabilities used by t-SNE. For each point i, nearby embeddings z j receive larger Gaussian weights, with sigma i setting the local neighborhood width; then the two directional probabilities for a pair are averaged and divided by two n to make symmetric pair probabilities. These probabilities describe local neighborhood structure, not physical distances directly.
items.evaluation-equation-c912f11bb8: These formulas define the pair probabilities in the two-dimensional t-SNE display, using the plotted coordinates y. Pairs that are close in the display get larger weights, and the denominator normalizes all distinct ordered pairs so the q values sum to one. The inverse one-plus-distance-squared weight has a heavier tail than a Gaussian, helping the layout separate clusters while fitting local neighborhoods.
items.evaluation-equation-07d4eff6d8: This energy is the squared distance between two latent vectors: the predictor’s next-state embedding from the current observation and action, and the encoder’s embedding of the actual next observation. A lower value means the transition is more compatible with the learned predictive constraint. Training must make observed transitions low energy while preventing trivial representations.
items.evaluation-equation-f4982b3079: This extends the predictive energy by adding xi, a latent variable for information not determined by the current observation and action. Different choices of xi can let the predictor match different compatible next observations, such as alternative futures at a fork. To be meaningful, xi must be constrained; otherwise it could encode the entire target and make the energy artificially small.
items.evaluation-equation-7f00fd6eef: This defines a conditional probability for an output y given an input x by turning lower energy E into larger weight through an exponential, then dividing by the total weight over all possible outputs u. The temperature tau is positive and controls sharpness: small tau favors the lowest energies more strongly. This step matters because an energy score becomes a probability only after this normalization is finite and positive.
items.evaluation-equation-34497fe863: This defines the asymmetric squared loss used for an expectile. The residual u is squared, but its weight depends on the sign: positive residuals get weight tau, while negative residuals get weight one minus tau. The condition that tau lies between zero and one keeps both sides meaningful and lets the loss emphasize underestimates or overestimates differently.
items.evaluation-equation-4fb8f12947: This is the balance condition for the value v that minimizes the asymmetric squared loss when the residual is Y minus v. The left side is the tau-weighted average amount by which targets Y sit above v; the right side is the one-minus-tau-weighted average amount by which targets sit below v. It shows that an expectile balances weighted magnitudes, not just how many samples fall on each side.
items.evaluation-equation-cc545bc5c6: This policy loss is a weighted imitation objective: it penalizes the squared difference between the policy’s predicted action pi of s and g and the dataset action a. The weight is an exponential of beta times the one-step advantage, so actions that look better than the current value prediction influence the fit more. This matters because the policy can favor promising observed actions without asking the offline value model to evaluate arbitrary new actions.
items.theory-equation-9f4544078d: This computes the least-squares coefficient for a one-coordinate probe using two fixed encoded inputs, negative one and positive one. Substituting targets equal to beta times the input plus noise leaves the true coefficient beta plus half the difference of the two noise terms. The calculation shows that even with the same frozen encoder, repeated noisy training samples produce different fitted probes.
items.theory-equation-3313ba4cd2: This identity decomposes the mean squared estimation error into squared bias plus estimator variance. It comes from adding and subtracting the average estimator, expanding the squared norm, and using the fact that the centered estimator has mean zero. The point is to separate systematic offset from variation across repeated training sets or noise draws.
items.theory-equation-852960f440: This is the ridge-regression estimator for a fixed design matrix X, where G is the feature Gram matrix X transpose X. The target vector y is multiplied by X transpose, and the inverse of G plus lambda times the identity applies regularized least squares. The regularization parameter lambda stabilizes directions with little data variation, but it also shrinks the fitted coefficient.
items.theory-equation-0e80790319: This gives the conditional bias of ridge regression when X is fixed and the noise has mean zero. Taking the expectation removes the noise term, and rewriting G as G plus lambda identity minus lambda identity leaves a negative shrinkage term applied to the true beta. In any eigen-direction of G, smaller data variation makes this shrinkage bias stronger.
items.theory-equation-0056f9c36e: Conditioning on the design matrix X, the noise has covariance sigma squared times the identity, so the covariance of beta hat is found by multiplying through G inverse, X transpose, the noise covariance, X, and G inverse. Since G is X transpose X, the middle factors collapse to G, leaving sigma squared times G inverse. This is the key step showing that weak Gram directions create large parameter variance.
items.theory-equation-412253a1ee: This is Cauchy–Schwarz applied to the two vectors with entries square root of rho j and one over square root of rho j. Their dot product is one added d times, so its square is d squared, and Cauchy bounds that by the product of the two squared lengths. With fixed total eigenvalue mass, it forces the reciprocal sum to be smallest when all eigenvalues match.
items.theory-equation-4c762a0033: The estimator m hat at query q predicts by giving each observed label Y i a kernel weight based on how close its stored representation Z i is to q. The numerator adds the weighted labels, and the denominator adds the weights so the result is an average when the denominator is positive. This formalizes the local smoothing used in the preceding example.
items.theory-equation-fb7563a4be: The population-smoothed target m h replaces the finite sample sums by density-weighted integrals around q. The numerator averages the conditional mean label m at nearby points q plus h u, weighted by the kernel and by how common those embeddings are; the denominator normalizes by the same local density mass. This target captures deterministic smoothing bias before finite-sample randomness is added.
items.theory-equation-2f064b404b: This Taylor expansion approximates a smooth function a near q after a small displacement h times u. It keeps the value at q, the first-order change from the gradient, the second-order curvature from the Hessian, and a remainder smaller than h squared in the limiting sense. This expansion is what lets the smoothing calculation isolate the leading bias terms.
items.theory-equation-1945bd6066: This formula gives the leading bias of the population-smoothed prediction m h at q compared with the true conditional mean m at q. The h squared term contains two effects: curvature of the label function, through the Laplacian of m, and asymmetric pulling by the embedding density, through the dot product of the label gradient with the density score grad log p. The remaining error is smaller than h squared as the bandwidth shrinks.
items.theory-equation-d0ece7856b: This ratio computes the expected squared radius of a uniformly chosen point inside a d-dimensional ball of radius r. The radial density is proportional to a to the d minus one, so the numerator adds squared radius times that radial weight and the denominator normalizes the weights. The result is d over d plus two times r squared, which then determines the coordinate variance by symmetry.
items.theory-equation-85a6c726d0: This is the small-radius bias for a fixed-radius neighbor average inside a ball. The leading r squared term again has a density-score contribution, grad m dot s, and a curvature contribution, one half the Laplacian of m, scaled by one over d plus two. It describes the population smoothing effect, assuming the local empirical neighborhood is sufficiently populated and regular.
items.theory-equation-452cd261e8: The location Fisher information, J of p, is the average squared length of the score, where the score is the gradient of the log density. Substituting score equals gradient of p divided by p turns that average into an integral of squared density-gradient length over the density. This measures how sensitive the density is to small location changes under the smooth positive-density assumptions used next.
items.theory-equation-fb521f3ebd: This identity says that the cross-moment between centered coordinate Z j and score coordinate s k is fixed: it is negative one when the coordinates match and zero otherwise. It comes from integration by parts, with the boundary term assumed to vanish, and it links the score to the covariance geometry used in the Fisher-information lower bound.
items.theory-equation-5bbf864c00: The expected squared length of the vector s of Z plus Sigma inverse times Z cannot be negative. Expanding it gives the Fisher information J of p, a cross term evaluated by the previous identity, and a quadratic covariance term, which combine to J of p minus the trace of Sigma inverse. Therefore J of p is at least the trace of Sigma inverse, with equality only in the Gaussian score case under the stated regularity assumptions.
items.theory-equation-71b38f1265: This bound controls the average square of the leading smoothing-bias expression, made from the Laplacian of the target function m and the dot product of its gradient with the score. The constants use the assumptions that the gradient of m is at most L and the Laplacian is at most B naught, plus the inequality for a squared sum and Cauchy–Schwarz. The density-dependent part enters through Fisher information J of p.
items.transformers-equation-6e75c421a7: An attention head forms queries, keys, and values by multiplying the token matrix X by three learned weight matrices. Each row of X is a token embedding, and these projections create three role-specific embeddings for attention: what a token seeks, how another token can be matched, and what content it offers. These are learned attention roles, not physical actions or observations.
items.transformers-equation-cb22318ab8: For token i, the output Y i is the sum of value vectors v j weighted by the attention weights A i j. In matrix form, all token outputs are A times V. Because each row of A comes from a softmax, this is a normalized weighted average of the value vectors for each query token.
items.transformers-equation-5fdfb014de: This derivative gives how one softmax weight A j changes when score S k is nudged. If j equals k, the weight increases by A j times one minus A j; if j is different from k, it decreases by A j times A k. The formula captures the competition among weights in the same row, since their total must remain one.
items.transformers-equation-843bd90adb: Layer Normalization takes one token vector, subtracts that token’s feature mean, divides by its feature standard deviation with epsilon for stability, then applies learned coordinatewise scale gamma and shift beta. The normalization is computed separately for each example or token across its features. This matters because before the learned affine step, it imposes per-example geometric constraints such as zero coordinate sum and a fixed normalized length when epsilon is zero.
items.transformers-equation-506e9e701f: The branch first layer-normalizes the current token features x, then uses the action embedding to choose a featurewise scale s and shift b, producing the action-conditioned representation r. A transformer sublayer F processes that representation, and its output is added back to x through a featurewise residual gate alpha, also chosen from the action. This matters because the action changes how the block processes the latent state without simply concatenating the action to every token.
items.paper-equation-7bc997b089: Equation 6 takes the batch of learned vectors and measures each one along a unit direction. Multiplying the feature axis of Z by u produces one scalar per example and time position; calling the result h does not make a new learned representation. Unit length keeps the measurement scale fixed when the direction changes. The paper prints this definition in Appendix A, and Equation 2 uses it.
items.paper-equation-cf1682b537: Equation 2 applies the one-dimensional normality discrepancy T to each projected batch, then averages those M scores. First choose unit directions; next project the batch along each direction; next compare each scalar distribution with the standard Gaussian; finally average. The theorem about all directions explains the ideal goal, but a finite set of directions and frequency nodes only approximates that goal.
items.paper-equation-1544d68410: Equation 3 is the full training tradeoff. The prediction term asks the shared encoder and predictor to agree about the next observation in latent space; the SIGReg term resists a constant or poorly spread embedding distribution. Lambda controls their relative weight. Both terms differentiate through the trainable encoder, but their numerical reductions in code determine what a given lambda actually means.
items.paper-equation-19aecf226e: Equation 4 scores a proposed plan by comparing its final predicted latent state with the encoded goal image. The squared Euclidean distance is small when those two vectors are close. This is a cost in learned coordinates, not a direct measurement of physical task success; it helps only if the embedding geometry preserves useful goal distinctions and the rollout is accurate.
items.paper-equation-be7f83adba: Equation 5 says to search over candidate action sequences and choose one with the lowest terminal latent cost from Equation 4. The model parameters stay fixed while actions are varied. The arg min denotes the action sequence, not the cost value. The paper uses compact horizon indices; our planning chapter makes the start-time offset explicit. CEM returns a good sampled candidate, not a proof of the global minimum.
